title: Big Feelings
objectives: I can name eight feelings that are stronger than happy or sad.
I can tell why a character feels a certain way.
I can use a feeling word to say how I felt and why.
I can tell how two feelings are alike and different.
rationale: Kindergarten and grade 1 gave children basic feelings. Second-grade stories and school days bring mixed feelings: wanting something and not getting it, making a mistake in front of others, a hard task, and the calm when a worry ends. The eight words split into feelings when something goes wrong (disappointed, embarrassed, frustrated, jealous), feelings of wanting to know or do (curious, eager), and good feelings after a worry or a kindness (relieved, grateful). Children use them to say how a character feels and why, which is the base of character thinking in later grades.

words.def: Sad because something hoped for did not happen.
words.ex: Ravi was disappointed when the picnic was canceled.
words.ex2: The team felt disappointed after losing the last game.
words.nonExample: Winning the prize you wanted is not a reason to feel disappointed.

apps.academic: A disappointed character hoped for something that did not happen.
apps.spoken: I was disappointed that it rained.
apps.writing: Use disappointed to show what a character hoped for and did not get.

cloze.s: Kai was ___ when the sunny field trip was moved indoors because of storms.

cloze2.s: The little girl was ___ that her balloon floated away before she could hold it.

misuse.s: Jada was disappointed because she won first prize and got the new bike she wanted.
misuse.why: Disappointed means sad that a hope did not happen, and winning a wanted prize is the opposite.

visual.alt: A sad child looking at rain falling on a picnic blanket.

words.def: Feeling shy and uncomfortable because of a mistake.
words.ex: Leo was embarrassed when he tripped in front of the class.
words.ex2: She felt embarrassed after she called her teacher Mom.
words.nonExample: Feeling proud of a good job is not feeling embarrassed.

apps.academic: An embarrassed character wants to hide after a mistake.
apps.spoken: I felt embarrassed when I forgot my line.
apps.writing: Use embarrassed to show a character who made a mistake in front of others.

cloze.s: Her face turned red, and she felt so ___ after she spilled juice on the new rug.

cloze2.s: Ben was ___ when his pants ripped in the middle of the school play.

misuse.s: The tall mountain was embarrassed because it was bigger than the hills.
misuse.why: Embarrassed is a feeling people have after a mistake, and a mountain cannot feel it.

visual.alt: A child with red cheeks beside a spilled cup.

words.def: Upset because something is hard or will not work.
words.ex: Nora was frustrated when the zipper got stuck again.
words.ex2: The frustrated boy could not find the last puzzle piece.
words.nonExample: Finishing an easy puzzle in one minute is not frustrating.

apps.academic: A frustrated learner may need a break or a new way to try.
apps.spoken: I am frustrated because the game will not load.
apps.writing: Use frustrated for a character who is upset because a task is too hard.

cloze.s: Carlos felt ___ after he tied his shoe five times and the knot came apart.

cloze2.s: The ___ cat scratched at the door because it would not open.

misuse.s: Rita felt frustrated because everything was easy and went just as she wanted.
misuse.why: Frustrated means upset when something is hard, and easy success does not cause it.

visual.alt: A child scrunching her face over a puzzle piece that does not fit.

words.def: Wanting to know or learn about something.
words.ex: The curious kitten sniffed every box in the room.
words.ex2: Ana was curious about what lived under the old log.
words.nonExample: Not caring what is inside a box is the opposite of being curious.

apps.academic: Curious scientists ask questions about what they see.
apps.spoken: I am curious about how seeds grow.
apps.writing: Use curious to show a character who wants to find out more.

cloze.s: The ___ boy opened the box slowly because he wanted to know what was inside.

cloze2.s: Mina was so ___ about the strange noise that she walked to the window to look.

misuse.s: The curious boy did not care what was inside the box and walked away.
misuse.why: Curious means wanting to know, and not caring is the opposite.

visual.alt: A kitten peeking into a box beside a magnifying glass.

words.def: Very excited and ready to do something.
words.ex: The eager students lined up before the museum doors opened.
words.ex2: Pablo was eager to show his grandmother the new puppy.
words.nonExample: Dragging your feet to do a chore is not being eager.

apps.academic: Eager readers ask for the next chapter.
apps.spoken: I am eager to start the game.
apps.writing: Use eager to show a character who cannot wait to begin.

cloze.s: The ___ runners crouched at the starting line, waiting for the signal.

cloze2.s: Lily was ___ to open her birthday present, so she tore the paper fast.

misuse.s: The eager boy yawned, sat down, and said he did not want to go on the fun trip.
misuse.why: Eager means excited and ready, and yawning and not wanting to go is the opposite.

visual.alt: A child jumping with arms up beside a packed backpack.

words.def: Happy because a worry has gone away.
words.ex: Jin felt relieved when he found his lost mitten.
words.ex2: The relieved girl smiled when the test was over.
words.nonExample: Staying worried all day is not feeling relieved.
words.rel: good feelings after a worry or a kindness

apps.academic: A relieved character no longer has to worry.
apps.spoken: I was so relieved when the bus came.
apps.writing: Use relieved to show the moment a character's worry ends.

cloze.s: Maya felt ___ when she found her lost dog safe in the neighbor's yard.

cloze2.s: After the loud thunder stopped, the ___ puppy crept out from under the bed.

misuse.s: Leo felt relieved because a big new worry started and his stomach hurt.
misuse.why: Relieved means a worry went away, and a new worry is the opposite.

visual.alt: A girl hugging her dog with a calm smile.

words.def: Unhappy because someone has something you want.
words.ex: Ben was jealous of his friend's new red bike.
words.ex2: Mia felt jealous when her brother got a puppy.
words.nonExample: Being glad for a friend who won is not being jealous.

apps.academic: A jealous character wants what someone else has.
apps.spoken: I felt jealous when my friend got the lead part.
apps.writing: Use jealous to explain a character's actions when someone else gets something good.

cloze.s: Tara felt ___ when her sister got the last cookie, because she wanted it too.

cloze2.s: The ___ little bird watched the other bird build a bigger nest.

misuse.s: Ben was jealous because his friend had nothing and he had everything.
misuse.why: Jealous means unhappy that someone has something you want, and here the friend has nothing.

visual.alt: A child looking sideways at a friend riding a shiny bike.

words.def: Thankful for something kind that someone did.
words.ex: Ruth was grateful for the warm soup on a cold day.
words.ex2: We are grateful to the crossing guard who helps us every day.
words.nonExample: Forgetting to say thank you does not show you are grateful.
words.rel: good feelings after a worry or a kindness

apps.academic: Grateful writers thank the people who helped them.
apps.spoken: I am grateful for your help.
apps.writing: Use grateful to show a character who feels thanks for a kind act.

cloze.s: I am ___ to my neighbor, who shoveled our snowy path before school.

cloze2.s: The ___ boy wrote a thank-you card to the nurse who helped him feel better.

misuse.s: Pia was grateful because her friend took her lunch and never gave it back.
misuse.why: Grateful means thankful for kindness, and taking her lunch is not kind.

visual.alt: A child holding a gift and smiling with hands pressed together.

passage.title: Nora's Kite
paras: Nora was eager to fly her new kite, but the string tangled and she grew frustrated. Her friends laughed, and she felt embarrassed.
A curious boy named Sam came to look. He fixed the knot, and Nora felt relieved. She was grateful for his help. When his kite flew higher, she was not jealous, and she was no longer disappointed.

qs.q: What does "frustrated" mean in the story?
qs.why: The string tangled, which made the kite hard to fly, so Nora felt upset.
Sam fixed the knot, so her worry went away.

qs.q: How did Nora feel about Sam at the end?
qs.why: She was grateful for his help and was not jealous.

write.prompt: Write or tell about a time you felt eager or relieved. What happened?

study.task: Sort the eight feeling words into feelings that feel good and feelings that feel hard. Choose one and show it with your face for a partner to guess.

groups.label: wanting to know or do something
good feelings after a worry or a kindness

sentences: Write a sentence about a time you felt disappointed.
Write a sentence that tells why a character might feel embarrassed.
Write a sentence about something you are grateful for and who gave it to you.

given: She wanted to go on the trip so much.
combine.model: Kim was eager to go on the trip while she waited for the bus.
Dad felt relieved when he found the missing keys.

discuss: Can a person feel curious and eager at the same time? Tell about a time.
How can a friend help when you feel frustrated?
produce.explain: Explain how disappointed and relieved are different feelings. Use both words.

argue.prompt: Is it okay to feel jealous? Say yes or no and give one reason.
argue.frame: I think it is ___ to feel jealous because ___.

constructed.prompt: Tell about a time something was hard and then got better. Use frustrated and relieved.
look: tells what happened first and then
constructed.model: I felt frustrated when my puzzle would not fit. I felt relieved when my friend showed me the last piece.

constructed.prompt: Write about a time someone helped you learn something. Use curious and grateful.
constructed.model: I was curious about how plants grow. I am grateful to my teacher, who let me plant a bean.

teacher.overview: Children learn eight feeling words that go beyond happy, sad, and mad, and use them to say why a character feels a certain way. Start with faces and situations, then add the words. The unit revisits complain, promise, and reply by asking how a character answers a feeling.

notes.va.disappointed.adj: Link to hoped-for events: the picnic was canceled, the game was lost. The word means a hope did not happen, not just sadness. Use a two-column chart: what I hoped and what happened.
notes.va.embarrassed.adj: Handle with care: do not ask children to share their own embarrassing moments. Use story characters and pictures. Clarify that everyone makes mistakes.
notes.va.frustrated.adj: Pair with a strategy: what could you try when you feel frustrated? Take a break, ask for help, try another way. Spanish speakers have the cognate frustrado.
notes.va.curious.adj: Link to science routines: What do you notice? What do you wonder? Curious means wanting to know, and it is a good thing in learning.
notes.va.eager.adj: Eager is excited and ready to start. Act out the difference between eager and unwilling. Eager can look like leaning forward or hands up.
notes.va.relieved.adj: Use a before and after: first a worry, then relief. Ask what the character was worried about. Relieved needs a worry to go away.
notes.va.jealous.adj: Jealous is wanting what someone else has; it is a normal feeling. Keep the focus on characters and talk about what to do with the feeling.
notes.va.grateful.adj: Link to thank-you notes. Grateful is about a kind act, not only a gift. Ask who a character is grateful to and why.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The kite string tangled and Nora could not fix it. That is hard, so she felt frustrated. Then Sam fixed it and her worry went away, so she felt relieved. I can say how she felt and why.'
discuss: Which feeling word fits when you wait for something you want a lot?
Which two feelings might a person have after a mistake?
misconceptions: Children may use embarrassed and ashamed as the same. Embarrassed is about being seen making a mistake; keep the focus light.
Some children think jealous is a bad feeling to have. It is a normal feeling; what a person does matters.
Children may think grateful is only said to a person who gave a gift. It also fits for kind acts and help.
extend: Make a class feelings chart with a picture and a sentence for each word.
Retell a story the class knows, naming how a character feels at the start and the end.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit complain, promise, and reply by asking what a frustrated character might complain about, what a grateful character might promise, and how a friend might reply.

wida.oral: Show a feeling with your face. Your partner says the feeling word and one reason a person might feel that way.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (decepcionado, avergonzado, frustrado, curioso, entusiasmado, aliviado, celoso, agradecido) not reviewed by a native speaker; entusiasmado for eager avoids ansioso, which can mean anxious.
